**40 practice questions: 28 multiple-choice (70%) + 12 short-response (30%).** Answers and explanations are collapsed initially. Every assigned lecture-review theme is represented either directly or through a closely aligned concept/application question.

# Part A — Multiple Choice

### Question 1 — Eye anatomy {#w06-mc01}

Which sequence correctly orders structures encountered by light entering the eye?

- **A.** retina → lens → cornea → pupil
- **B.** cornea → aqueous humor → pupil → lens → retina
- **C.** lens → cornea → retina → pupil
- **D.** pupil → optic nerve → lens → cornea

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**

Cornea → aqueous humor → pupil → lens → vitreous → retina.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
**B follows the physical path of incoming light through the eye.** Light first crosses the cornea, then the aqueous humor of the anterior part of the eye, passes through the pupil, and reaches the lens. After the lens it travels through the vitreous humor before reaching the retina. The option omits the vitreous but preserves the correct order of the listed structures.

The cornea supplies much of the eye's refraction; the pupil is an adjustable opening that controls how much light enters; the lens fine-tunes focus; and retinal photoreceptors convert light into electrical responses.

The other sequences place structures in an anatomically impossible order or send light through the optic nerve. The optic nerve carries electrical output from retinal ganglion cells after retinal processing; it is not the route by which external light reaches the retina.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 2 — Refraction {#w06-mc02}

Refraction occurs when light:

- **A.** changes speed and direction at a boundary between media
- **B.** generates an action potential in the optic nerve
- **C.** activates a motor unit
- **D.** is converted to sound

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

Refraction is bending associated with a change in propagation speed between media.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
**Refraction is an optical event at a boundary between media with different refractive indices**, making A the intended answer. When a light ray crosses such a boundary obliquely, its change in propagation speed is accompanied by a change in direction. Curved corneal and lens surfaces use this effect to bend incoming rays so that an image can be focused on the retina.

A useful qualification is that a ray striking a boundary exactly along the normal can change speed without changing direction.

Generating an action potential in the optic nerve occurs after retinal transduction and processing, so B is not refraction. Motor-unit activation concerns skeletal muscle, and light is not normally converted into sound by the eye.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 3 — Accommodation {#w06-mc03}

During accommodation for near vision, the lens becomes:

- **A.** flatter
- **B.** rounder/more convex
- **C.** opaque
- **D.** displaced into the retina

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**

Ciliary-muscle contraction allows the lens to become rounder.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Light from a nearby object reaches the eye as more strongly diverging rays than light from a distant object. To focus those rays on the same retina, the eye needs greater refractive power. A **rounder, more convex lens** provides that increased power, so B is correct.

Near accommodation begins when the ciliary muscle contracts. Because it is arranged as a ring, contraction reduces tension in the zonular fibers that suspend the lens. With less outward pull, the lens's own elasticity allows it to become rounder.

A flatter lens in A has less refractive power and is associated with distant rather than near focus. Becoming opaque would obstruct vision, not focus the image. The lens also does not move into the retina as in D.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 4 — Presbyopia {#w06-mc04}

Presbyopia is primarily a loss of:

- **A.** retinal rods
- **B.** accommodation with age
- **C.** auditory hair cells
- **D.** skeletal muscle Ca2+ stores

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**

Presbyopia is age-related loss of near focusing/accommodation.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
**Presbyopia is the age-related reduction in accommodation**, especially the ability to focus on nearby objects, so B is correct. Near vision requires the lens to become more curved when zonular tension decreases. With age, the lens becomes less able to change shape, so the increase in refractive power available for close work becomes smaller.

The ciliary muscle may still receive the appropriate command, but a less flexible lens cannot respond with the same shape change. An image can therefore be poorly focused on otherwise functioning photoreceptors.

Loss of retinal rods in A would primarily concern light detection, particularly in dim conditions, rather than defining presbyopia. Auditory hair cells in C belong to hearing, and skeletal muscle calcium stores in D belong to contraction.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 5 — Photoreceptors {#w06-mc05}

Which photoreceptor is best suited for dim-light vision?

- **A.** cone
- **B.** rod
- **C.** ganglion cell
- **D.** bipolar cell

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**

Rods are highly sensitive and support dim-light vision.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
**Rods are better suited to dim-light vision**, making B correct. Their phototransduction machinery is highly sensitive, and rod pathways can pool signals from multiple receptors. That combination allows weak illumination to be detected when cone-mediated vision is less effective.

Extensive convergence reduces the precision with which the pathway can identify the exact photoreceptor stimulated, and rods do not provide the comparisons among cone classes needed for normal color discrimination. Cones are more important for detailed, color-rich vision under brighter conditions.

Bipolar cells and ordinary retinal ganglion cells are downstream components of retinal processing, not the rod or cone photoreceptors being compared here. Some ganglion cells have specialized intrinsic light sensitivity, but that does not make them the answer to a question about ordinary dim-light image vision.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 6 — Fovea {#w06-mc06}

High visual acuity in the fovea is associated with:

- **A.** dense cones and low convergence
- **B.** only rods and high convergence
- **C.** no ganglion cells
- **D.** absence of photoreceptors

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

The fovea has dense cones and relatively little convergence.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
High acuity means resolving fine spatial detail, not simply detecting that light is present. The fovea contains densely packed cones with relatively low convergence in its high-acuity pathways, so **A is correct**. Information from neighboring cones remains more distinct, allowing the CNS to distinguish closely spaced features in an image.

By comparison, when many photoreceptors converge onto a smaller number of downstream channels, weak signals can be pooled, improving sensitivity. However, the output becomes less precise about which receptor contributed.

The foveal center is not a rod-only region, so B reverses the relevant specialization. Absence of ganglion-cell output in C would prevent normal retinal communication with the brain, rather than explain high acuity. Absence of photoreceptors in D describes a failure of light detection, not fine vision.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 7 — Phototransduction {#w06-mc07}

In a rod exposed to light, cGMP concentration falls and cation channels:

- **A.** open, depolarizing the cell
- **B.** close, hyperpolarizing the cell
- **C.** become nicotinic receptors
- **D.** release Ca2+ from skeletal SR

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**

Light closes cyclic-nucleotide-gated channels and hyperpolarizes rods.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
**B is correct: light lowers cGMP, closes cyclic-nucleotide-gated cation channels, and hyperpolarizes the rod.** Begin with the dark state. In darkness, relatively high cGMP keeps these outer-segment channels open, allowing an inward current that helps maintain the rod at a relatively depolarized voltage.

Light activates rhodopsin, which activates transducin and then phosphodiesterase. Phosphodiesterase breaks down cGMP, so more cation channels close. With less inward positive current while outward K⁺ current continues, the membrane becomes more negative. This hyperpolarization reduces calcium entry at the synaptic terminal and decreases glutamate release.

Option A describes the wrong direction of channel movement and voltage change. The channels do not become nicotinic receptors, and skeletal sarcoplasmic-reticulum calcium release is unrelated to this receptor mechanism.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 8 — Dark current {#w06-mc08}

In darkness, rods are relatively depolarized because:

- **A.** cGMP-gated cation channels are open
- **B.** all K+ channels are closed forever
- **C.** rhodopsin is maximally active
- **D.** ACh opens nicotinic receptors

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

High cGMP keeps cation channels open in darkness.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
In darkness, cGMP remains sufficiently high to keep many outer-segment cyclic-nucleotide-gated cation channels open. Their inward current contributes to a relatively depolarized rod membrane potential, making **A correct**. This continuing current is called the **dark current**; darkness is therefore not an electrically inactive state for the photoreceptor.

The depolarized state supports ongoing calcium entry at the synaptic terminal and tonic glutamate release. When light closes the cGMP-gated channels, the inward current decreases and the rod hyperpolarizes, reducing transmitter release.

Option B is incorrect because outward potassium current remains part of the membrane-current balance. Rhodopsin is activated by light rather than being maximally active in darkness, so C reverses the trigger. Acetylcholine acting at nicotinic receptors in D describes neuromuscular transmission, not the source of the rod's dark current.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 9 — Visual pathway {#w06-mc09}

Fibers from the nasal half of each retina:

- **A.** never leave the eye
- **B.** cross at the optic chiasm
- **C.** project directly to spinal cord
- **D.** become motor neurons

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**

Nasal retinal fibers cross at the optic chiasm.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
**B is correct: axons from the nasal half of each retina cross at the optic chiasm.** Axons from the temporal half remain on the same side.

Because the eye's optics reverse the image, a particular visual hemifield falls on complementary halves of the two retinas. Information about the left visual field reaches the right hemisphere, and information about the right visual field reaches the left hemisphere. Each hemisphere can therefore combine information about the same side of visual space from both eyes.

The fibers do leave the eye in the optic nerve, so A is incorrect. The major conscious visual pathway proceeds toward thalamic and cortical targets rather than directly into the spinal cord, and these retinal ganglion-cell axons do not become motor neurons.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 10 — NMJ {#w06-mc10}

At the neuromuscular junction, ACh binds primarily to:

- **A.** muscarinic M2 receptors
- **B.** nicotinic ligand-gated cation channels
- **C.** alpha1 adrenergic receptors
- **D.** rhodopsin

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**

Skeletal muscle motor end plates use nicotinic ACh receptors.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
At the skeletal neuromuscular junction, acetylcholine binds **nicotinic ACh receptors**, which are ligand-gated, nonselective cation channels. **B is correct.** At the muscle fiber's resting membrane potential, opening these channels produces a net inward positive current, mainly because sodium entry exceeds the opposing potassium movement. This depolarization is the end-plate potential.

The end-plate potential is graded. If it brings adjacent excitable membrane to threshold, voltage-gated sodium channels generate an all-or-none muscle action potential. The nicotinic receptor therefore initiates the local depolarization but is not itself the voltage-gated channel responsible for propagating the muscle action potential.

Muscarinic M2 receptors in A are important in parasympathetic cardiac signalling, not the skeletal motor end plate. Alpha1 receptors in C respond to adrenergic signalling, and rhodopsin in D initiates phototransduction.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 11 — NMJ release {#w06-mc11}

A motor-neuron action potential triggers ACh release by opening terminal:

- **A.** voltage-gated Ca2+ channels
- **B.** ligand-gated Cl− channels
- **C.** funny channels
- **D.** gap junctions

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

Presynaptic Ca²⁺ entry triggers vesicle fusion.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
An arriving motor-neuron action potential depolarizes the presynaptic terminal and opens **voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels**, making A correct. Calcium enters down its electrochemical gradient, raising local cytosolic calcium near docked synaptic vesicles. Calcium-sensitive release machinery then promotes vesicle fusion and acetylcholine exocytosis into the synaptic cleft.

Acetylcholine subsequently binds receptors on the muscle membrane, but that postsynaptic event occurs after the presynaptic calcium entry tested here.

Ligand-gated chloride channels in B do not provide this exocytotic trigger. Funny channels in C contribute to cardiac pacemaker activity rather than neuromuscular transmitter release. Gap junctions in D permit direct current flow between coupled cells; the skeletal neuromuscular junction is a chemical synapse instead.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 12 — Sarcomere {#w06-mc12}

A sarcomere extends from:

- **A.** one Z disc to the next Z disc
- **B.** one motor neuron to another
- **C.** the SR to the sarcolemma
- **D.** one tendon to another

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

The sarcomere is the repeating unit between Z discs.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
A **sarcomere runs from one Z disc to the next**, so A is correct. It is the repeating contractile unit within a myofibril. Thin actin filaments attach to the Z discs and extend toward the center, while thick myosin filaments occupy the central region around the M line.

During shortening, thin filaments slide farther between thick filaments and the Z discs move closer together. The sarcomere becomes shorter even though the filaments themselves remain essentially the same length.

The other options confuse levels of organization. Motor neurons are nerve cells, the sarcoplasmic reticulum and sarcolemma are membrane systems, and tendons attach whole muscles to other structures. None of those pairs defines the boundaries of one repeating myofibrillar unit.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 13 — SR {#w06-mc13}

The sarcoplasmic reticulum is specialized primarily for:

- **A.** storing and releasing Ca2+
- **B.** synthesizing ACh
- **C.** carrying oxygen
- **D.** detecting sound

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

The SR is the major intracellular Ca²⁺ store in skeletal muscle.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The **sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR)** is a specialized intracellular membrane network that stores and releases calcium, making A correct. At rest, most calcium needed for activation is stored outside the cytosol. Excitation–contraction coupling opens SR release channels, allowing cytosolic Ca²⁺ to rise quickly and activate the contractile machinery.

Relaxation requires the reverse movement. SERCA pumps use ATP to return calcium to the SR, lowering its cytosolic concentration so that calcium dissociates from troponin and cross-bridge activation declines.

Acetylcholine is synthesized and released by the motor-neuron terminal, not primarily by the muscle SR. Oxygen transport belongs mainly to blood and oxygen-binding proteins, while sound detection belongs to sensory receptors. Do not confuse the SR with T-tubules: **the SR supplies stored calcium; T-tubules carry membrane depolarization into the fiber**.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 14 — T-tubules {#w06-mc14}

T-tubules are important because they:

- **A.** bring the muscle action potential deep into the fiber
- **B.** store hemoglobin
- **C.** synthesize ATP only
- **D.** form the myelin sheath

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

T-tubules conduct depolarization into the muscle cell interior.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
A signal confined to a muscle fiber's surface would not efficiently activate its internal myofibrils. **T-tubules carry the muscle action potential deep into the fiber**, making A correct. They are inward extensions of the sarcolemma, with their lumen continuous with extracellular space.

At triads, a T-tubule lies next to terminal cisternae of the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Depolarization activates voltage sensors in the T-tubule membrane, which are coupled to calcium-release channels in the nearby SR. This arrangement allows a surface electrical event to trigger coordinated calcium release throughout the cell.

T-tubules do not store hemoglobin, function only as ATP-producing structures, or form myelin. They also should not be described as the main calcium-storage compartment: that is the SR.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 15 — Regulation {#w06-mc15}

Ca2+ initiates skeletal muscle contraction by binding to:

- **A.** myosin ATPase directly
- **B.** troponin
- **C.** titin
- **D.** nebulin

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**

Ca²⁺ binds troponin, moving tropomyosin away from actin binding sites.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
**Ca²⁺ binds troponin**, specifically its calcium-binding component, so B is correct. This binding changes the conformation of the troponin complex and shifts the associated tropomyosin on the thin filament. Myosin-binding sites on actin become more accessible, allowing cross-bridges to form and cycle.

Calcium therefore acts as a **regulatory signal**: it permits the motor proteins to interact. It does not replace ATP as the energy source, and it does not need to bind directly to myosin ATPase to initiate the normal skeletal-muscle regulatory sequence.

Titin in C contributes elastic and structural support, including stabilization of thick filaments. Nebulin in D helps organize thin filaments. Neither is the main calcium-sensitive switch identified in this question.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 16 — Cross-bridge cycle {#w06-mc16}

ATP binding to myosin is required primarily for:

- **A.** detachment of myosin from actin
- **B.** exposing the actin site by binding troponin
- **C.** opening nicotinic receptors
- **D.** producing the motor-neuron AP

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

ATP binding causes cross-bridge detachment.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The question specifically asks about **ATP binding**, not ATP hydrolysis. When a new ATP molecule binds to myosin, myosin's affinity for actin decreases and the cross-bridge detaches. **A is correct.** Hydrolysis of that ATP subsequently places the myosin head in an energized, re-cocked state that can participate in another cycle.

If actin sites remain available because calcium is still bound to troponin, the head can reattach. Release of inorganic phosphate is associated with the force-generating transition, and ADP is released as the cycle proceeds.

Calcium, not ATP binding to troponin, exposes the binding sites. Nicotinic receptors respond to ACh, and a motor-neuron action potential is a separate electrical process. In the absence of ATP, attached cross-bridges cannot detach normally, contributing to rigor.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 17 — Sliding filament {#w06-mc17}

During skeletal muscle shortening:

- **A.** actin and myosin filaments themselves shorten substantially
- **B.** thin filaments slide past thick filaments, increasing overlap
- **C.** Z discs move farther apart
- **D.** sarcomeres disappear

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**

Filaments slide; sarcomeres shorten.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
**B describes the sliding-filament mechanism.** Thin actin filaments move relative to thick myosin filaments, increasing overlap and bringing the Z discs closer together. The sarcomere shortens because its internal components slide past one another, not because each actin or myosin filament contracts like a shrinking rope.

The A band, which corresponds to thick-filament length, remains approximately constant. The I band and H zone become narrower as shortening increases overlap.

Option A incorrectly shortens the filaments themselves. Option C moves the Z discs in the direction of stretching rather than shortening. Sarcomeres remain present, so D is not a description of normal contraction. Also remember that the term **contraction** can mean force production without whole-muscle shortening; this question specifically describes the shortening situation.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 18 — E-C coupling {#w06-mc18}

In skeletal muscle, the voltage sensor that responds to T-tubule depolarization is functionally linked to:

- **A.** ryanodine receptors in the SR
- **B.** baroreceptors
- **C.** olfactory GPCRs
- **D.** erythropoietin receptors

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

T-tubule voltage sensors activate SR ryanodine receptors.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
**A is correct because the T-tubule voltage sensor is coupled to ryanodine receptors in the sarcoplasmic reticulum.** In skeletal muscle, depolarization changes the conformation of the dihydropyridine receptor, an L-type calcium-channel protein that acts as the voltage sensor. Mechanical coupling to the SR ryanodine receptor allows stored calcium to be released into the cytosol.

That calcium then binds troponin and permits cross-bridge cycling.

A particularly important distinction is that normal skeletal-muscle coupling does not require extracellular calcium entry through the L-type channel to provide the immediate trigger in the way cardiac coupling does. Baroreceptors, olfactory GPCRs, and erythropoietin receptors belong to other physiological systems and cannot fill this role. Locate each component correctly: **voltage sensing in the T-tubule membrane; calcium release from the SR membrane**.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 19 — Relaxation {#w06-mc19}

Skeletal muscle relaxation requires:

- **A.** persistent high cytosolic Ca2+
- **B.** SERCA-mediated Ca2+ uptake into SR
- **C.** continuous ACh release
- **D.** irreversible actin breakdown

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**

SERCA lowers cytosolic Ca²⁺ by pumping it back into SR.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Relaxation requires cytosolic calcium to decline so that it dissociates from troponin. **SERCA pumps move Ca²⁺ from the cytosol back into the SR using ATP**, making B correct. As troponin returns toward its resting state, tropomyosin again restricts access to myosin-binding sites on actin, reducing further cross-bridge formation.

Stopping motor-neuron firing prevents further excitation, but the calcium already released must still be removed. Existing cross-bridges also require ATP-dependent detachment as the muscle returns toward the resting state.

Persistently high cytosolic calcium in A would maintain activation rather than promote relaxation. Continued ACh release in C would tend to produce further muscle excitation. Actin is not irreversibly destroyed during each normal contraction–relaxation cycle, so D is wrong.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 20 — Twitch {#w06-mc20}

A single skeletal muscle action potential normally produces:

- **A.** a twitch
- **B.** a cardiac cycle
- **C.** tetanus immediately
- **D.** an ECG P wave

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

A single excitation produces a brief twitch response.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
A single action potential in a resting skeletal muscle fiber normally initiates one brief contraction–relaxation response called a **twitch**, so A is correct. The electrical event first triggers SR calcium release. Calcium activates troponin, cross-bridges generate force, and subsequent calcium reuptake allows the force to decline.

The mechanical response lasts longer than the membrane action potential because calcium handling and cross-bridge cycling continue after the brief electrical event has ended.

Tetanus in C requires sufficiently frequent repeated stimulation, not one isolated action potential. A cardiac cycle and an ECG P wave describe events in the heart rather than a skeletal fiber's twitch. Force can be adjusted through stimulation frequency, motor-unit recruitment, muscle length, and other mechanical conditions.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 21 — Summation {#w06-mc21}

Temporal summation occurs when:

- **A.** a second stimulus arrives before the muscle has fully relaxed
- **B.** all motor units are silent
- **C.** the sarcomere is infinitely long
- **D.** the optic nerve is cut

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

Residual Ca²⁺/force allows the next twitch to add to the previous one.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
**Temporal summation occurs when another stimulus arrives before the muscle has fully relaxed**, making A correct. The second muscle action potential triggers additional calcium release while some calcium and force from the first response remain.

What sums is the **mechanical response and its calcium-dependent activation**, not the amplitudes of overlapping action potentials. At sufficiently high stimulation rates, relaxation between responses becomes incomplete and eventually the force can become smoothly sustained in fused tetanus.

Silent motor units in B cannot generate the repeated active response. An infinitely long sarcomere in C is neither physiological nor a requirement for summation, and cutting the optic nerve in D is unrelated. Keep temporal summation separate from recruitment: summation changes the timing of activity in already active fibers, whereas recruitment adds more motor units to the contraction.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 22 — Motor unit {#w06-mc22}

A motor unit consists of:

- **A.** one motor neuron and all skeletal muscle fibers it innervates
- **B.** one sarcomere and one tendon
- **C.** one sensory neuron and one receptor
- **D.** one atrium and ventricle

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

One alpha motor neuron plus its muscle fibers forms a motor unit.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
A **motor unit consists of one alpha motor neuron and all the skeletal muscle fibers it innervates**, so A is correct. When that neuron generates an action potential, its branches deliver the signal to the neuromuscular junctions of the fibers in its unit, allowing them to contribute to the muscle's response.

Activating additional units increases the number of contracting fibers and therefore can increase total force. Small units allow fine increments of force, while larger units can make greater contributions when substantial force is needed.

A sarcomere and tendon in B belong to different structural levels and do not define a neural control unit. A sensory neuron and receptor in C describe an afferent arrangement, not motor output. An atrium and ventricle in D are cardiac chambers.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 23 — Recruitment {#w06-mc23}

According to the size principle, increasing force generally recruits:

- **A.** large motor units before small ones
- **B.** small motor units before larger ones
- **C.** all units simultaneously
- **D.** only sensory neurons

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**

Small, fatigue-resistant motor units are generally recruited first.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The **size principle** describes the usual order in which motor units are recruited as neural drive increases: smaller, lower-threshold motor neurons tend to be activated before larger ones. **B is correct.** Small motor units are often associated with fatigue-resistant fibers and make relatively modest increments of force, which is useful for posture and precise movement.

As the demand for force rises, additional and progressively larger motor units are brought into activity. The nervous system can simultaneously increase firing rates in already recruited units, so recruitment and frequency coding can cooperate.

Option A reverses the usual order. Option C removes the graded control that orderly recruitment provides; activating every unit at once would make fine adjustment difficult. Sensory neurons in D carry input and are not the motor units being recruited.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 24 — Length-tension {#w06-mc24}

Active force is reduced when a sarcomere is stretched far beyond optimal length because:

- **A.** actin–myosin overlap becomes too small
- **B.** ATP cannot bind myosin
- **C.** motor neurons stop releasing ACh permanently
- **D.** the SR becomes the nucleus

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

Too little filament overlap limits cross-bridge formation.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
When a sarcomere is stretched far beyond its optimal length, thick and thin filaments overlap less. Fewer myosin heads can reach available actin sites, so fewer force-generating cross-bridges can operate. **A is correct.** The limiting factor is the geometry of the contractile apparatus, not a necessary failure of ATP binding or neurotransmitter release.

At the opposite extreme, a very short sarcomere also generates less active force because excessive thin-filament overlap and interference with the thick filaments impair useful force generation. Between those extremes, an optimal range of overlap allows many effective cross-bridges.

This question asks about **active force**. Passive tension from elastic structures such as titin and connective tissue can rise as the muscle is stretched even while active force declines. The other options propose unrelated or impossible changes rather than explaining the length–tension relationship.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 25 — Muscle hierarchy {#w06-mc25}

Which order is correct from largest to smallest?

- **A.** muscle → fascicle → fiber → myofibril → sarcomere
- **B.** sarcomere → muscle → fiber → fascicle
- **C.** myofibril → muscle → sarcomere → fiber
- **D.** fiber → muscle → fascicle → sarcomere

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

Whole muscle contains fascicles, fibers, myofibrils, and sarcomeres.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
**A gives the correct structural hierarchy:** a whole muscle contains fascicles; each fascicle contains muscle fibers; each fiber contains myofibrils; and each myofibril contains sarcomeres arranged in series. A skeletal muscle fiber is one long, multinucleated cell, not a bundle of smaller muscle cells.

Inside each sarcomere are the thick and thin filaments that interact to generate force. Thus the hierarchy connects the visible organ to the microscopic repeating machinery responsible for contraction. Connective tissue organizes the larger levels and helps transmit force, while the sarcolemma and internal membrane systems belong to the individual muscle fiber.

The other sequences mix levels in impossible orders, such as placing the entire muscle inside a myofibril or a sarcomere above a whole muscle.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 26 — Protein function {#w06-mc26}

Which protein is the motor protein that forms cross-bridges and performs the power stroke?

- **A.** actin
- **B.** myosin
- **C.** tropomyosin
- **D.** titin

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**

Myosin is the ATPase motor protein.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
**Myosin is the motor protein**, making B correct. Its heads contain actin-binding sites and ATPase activity. They interact with actin and undergo conformational changes during the cross-bridge cycle, converting chemical energy into mechanical force and, when the load permits, movement.

Actin in A forms the main structural backbone of thin filaments and provides binding sites for myosin, but it is not the ATPase motor responsible for the power stroke. Tropomyosin in C regulates access to those binding sites. Titin in D contributes elastic support and helps organize and stabilize the thick filament within the sarcomere.

Calcium binding to troponin controls whether myosin can interact effectively with actin, while ATP supports the myosin cycle.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 27 — Visual coding {#w06-mc27}

Convergence of many photoreceptors onto fewer retinal neurons generally:

- **A.** increases sensitivity but reduces spatial acuity
- **B.** reduces sensitivity and increases color vision always
- **C.** has no effect
- **D.** creates muscle tetanus

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

Convergence trades spatial detail for sensitivity.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Convergence means that signals from multiple photoreceptors are combined into fewer downstream channels. Pooling can make a weak light stimulus more detectable because small inputs contribute to a shared response. However, the output carries less precise information about which individual photoreceptor was stimulated. **A correctly states the trade-off: greater sensitivity but lower spatial acuity.**

Imagine two adjacent receptors feeding one output channel. Activity in that channel indicates light somewhere in their combined receptive field, but may not distinguish which of the two received it.

This helps explain the contrast between highly convergent rod pathways and the lower-convergence, high-acuity cone pathways of the fovea. Convergence does not automatically improve color vision, have no effect, or produce a muscular event.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 28 — Integration {#w06-mc28}

A drug that competitively blocks nicotinic ACh receptors at the NMJ would most directly cause:

- **A.** failure of end-plate depolarization and weakness
- **B.** increased rod sensitivity
- **C.** hypertension by alpha1 activation
- **D.** increased erythropoiesis

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

Blocking nicotinic receptors prevents normal end-plate potentials.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The toxin's specified target is the **postsynaptic nicotinic ACh receptor**, so A is the most direct consequence. The motor neuron can still generate an action potential and may release ACh normally, but fewer functional receptors are available to produce the end-plate current. The resulting end-plate potential is reduced and may fail to reach the threshold for a muscle action potential.

If a muscle action potential does not occur, T-tubule depolarization and normal SR calcium release do not follow. Troponin is not adequately activated, and the fiber contributes less or no force. The effect depends on the extent of receptor blockade; a partial block need not abolish every response immediately.

The other alternatives concern rods, alpha1-mediated vascular responses, or red-cell production and do not follow directly from blocking skeletal-muscle nicotinic receptors.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

# Part B — Short Response

### Question 29 — Optics {#w06-sr01}

Explain accommodation for near vision and why presbyopia develops.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Near focus: ciliary muscle contracts, zonular tension falls, lens rounds and refractive power increases; presbyopia reflects reduced lens elasticity with age.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Near vision requires greater refractive power because rays arriving from a nearby object diverge more strongly. The eye achieves this through **accommodation**, in which the shape of the lens changes while the retina remains in its position at the back of the eye.

For near focus, the ciliary muscle contracts. Its ring-like arrangement means that contraction reduces the pull exerted through the zonular fibers. Once that tension decreases, the lens's elasticity allows it to become rounder and more convex. The increased curvature bends incoming rays more strongly, helping bring the near object's image into focus on the retina. For distant focus, ciliary relaxation increases zonular tension and the lens becomes flatter.

Presbyopia develops as the lens becomes less flexible with age. Even when the ciliary muscle changes tension appropriately, the lens cannot increase its curvature as effectively. The range of near focusing therefore decreases. This is a limitation of optical accommodation, not necessarily a loss of photoreceptor sensitivity.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 30 — Retina {#w06-sr02}

Compare rods and cones in sensitivity, acuity, color, and retinal distribution.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Rods: high sensitivity, dim light, no color, lower acuity, more peripheral; cones: lower sensitivity, color, high acuity, dense in fovea.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
**Rods are highly sensitive** and support vision in dim light, but they do not supply the comparisons among cone classes required for normal color discrimination. Rod pathways also tend to pool information from many receptors, so their excellent sensitivity comes at the cost of spatial detail.

**Cones function best at brighter light levels** and support color vision through comparisons among cone types with different spectral sensitivities. In high-acuity regions, particularly the fovea, cones are densely packed and their signals undergo relatively little convergence. Keeping neighboring inputs distinct allows the visual system to resolve fine detail.

Cones are especially concentrated in the fovea, while rods are abundant outside the foveal center and are absent from its very center. Neither receptor type should be described as occupying only one absolute half of the retina: the distinction is a pattern of density and specialization.

More pooling helps detect weak light but obscures the exact receptor of origin, whereas low convergence supports fine spatial discrimination under conditions in which individual cone signals are sufficiently strong.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 31 — Phototransduction {#w06-sr03}

Trace rod phototransduction from photon absorption to altered glutamate release.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Photon → rhodopsin activation → transducin → phosphodiesterase → ↓cGMP → cation channels close → hyperpolarization → ↓glutamate release.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
In darkness, cGMP keeps outer-segment cyclic-nucleotide-gated cation channels open. Their inward current helps keep the rod relatively depolarized, supporting ongoing calcium entry at the synaptic terminal and tonic glutamate release.

A photon is absorbed by the retinal component of rhodopsin, producing a conformational change that activates the pigment. Activated rhodopsin stimulates the G protein transducin, which activates phosphodiesterase. Phosphodiesterase breaks down cGMP, so cGMP concentration falls and the cation channels close.

The reduction in inward positive current, while outward potassium current continues, makes the rod membrane more negative: it **hyperpolarizes**. This reduces activation of synaptic voltage-gated calcium channels and therefore reduces glutamate release. The receptor response is graded rather than an action potential of fixed amplitude.

Retinal circuits then interpret the change in glutamate. ON and OFF pathways respond differently, so reduced rod transmitter release should not be summarized as every downstream neuron becoming less active. Retinal ganglion cells ultimately encode processed visual information in spikes.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 32 — Visual pathway {#w06-sr04}

Trace the major visual pathway and explain the significance of the optic chiasm.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Retina/ganglion cells → optic nerves → partial crossing of nasal fibers at optic chiasm → optic tracts → LGN → visual cortex.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The major image-forming pathway begins with photoreceptors signalling through retinal circuits to **ganglion cells**. Ganglion-cell axons form the optic nerve. At the optic chiasm, fibers from each nasal hemiretina cross, while fibers from each temporal hemiretina remain on the same side. Beyond the chiasm, these axons form the optic tracts.

The major pathway then relays in the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus and continues through optic radiations to primary visual cortex. Additional retinal projections support functions such as reflexes, but they are not substitutes for this principal conscious-vision pathway.

Because the eye reverses the image optically, the left visual field is represented on complementary retinal halves in the two eyes. Crossing only the nasal fibers brings those signals together in the right hemisphere. The reverse arrangement applies to the right visual field and left hemisphere.

Avoid saying that all optic fibers cross or that one hemisphere receives the complete visual world from only one eye.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 33 — NMJ {#w06-sr05}

Trace neuromuscular transmission from motor-neuron action potential to muscle-fiber action potential.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
AP → presynaptic Ca²⁺ entry → ACh release → nicotinic receptor opening → end-plate potential → voltage-gated Na⁺ channels → muscle AP.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
An action potential reaches the motor-neuron terminal and opens presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels. The resulting calcium entry triggers vesicle fusion and release of **acetylcholine (ACh)** into the synaptic cleft. ACh diffuses to the motor end plate, where it binds nicotinic receptors on the muscle membrane.

These receptors are ligand-gated cation channels. At the resting muscle potential, their opening produces a net inward positive current and a local **end-plate potential**. That potential is graded: its size depends on the effective synaptic current. If it depolarizes adjacent membrane to threshold, voltage-gated sodium channels open and generate the muscle action potential.

The muscle action potential propagates along the sarcolemma and T-tubules, providing the excitation needed for later calcium release and contraction. Acetylcholinesterase breaks down ACh in the cleft, helping terminate the synaptic signal; transmitter removal should not be confused with the subsequent removal of calcium from muscle cytosol.

The nerve's action potential does not simply jump across the cleft unchanged.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 34 — Sarcomere {#w06-sr06}

Describe sarcomere organization and the roles of actin, myosin, troponin, tropomyosin, titin, and nebulin.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Actin thin filaments anchor at Z discs; myosin forms thick filaments; troponin/tropomyosin regulate binding; titin provides elasticity/centering; nebulin supports thin-filament organization.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
A sarcomere extends from one Z disc to the next. Thin filaments contain **actin** and anchor at the Z discs, extending inward toward the center. Thick filaments contain **myosin** and occupy the central region around the M line. Myosin heads bind actin and use ATP-dependent cycling to generate force.

The thin filament also carries the regulatory proteins **troponin and tropomyosin**. At low cytosolic calcium, tropomyosin restricts myosin's access to actin-binding sites. Calcium binding to troponin changes the regulatory complex and shifts tropomyosin, allowing effective cross-bridge formation.

**Titin** is a large elastic protein extending between the Z-disc region and the central thick-filament region. It helps position and stabilize myosin and contributes passive elasticity. **Nebulin** lies along the thin filament and supports its organization and alignment. Neither should be confused with the ATPase motor or the main calcium-sensitive switch.

Filament overlap determines how many cross-bridges can operate, regulatory proteins determine whether access is permitted, and structural proteins help maintain alignment and elastic behavior.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 35 — Cross-bridge cycle {#w06-sr07}

Describe one complete cross-bridge cycle and the roles of Ca²⁺ and ATP.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Ca²⁺ exposes actin sites; energized myosin binds actin, power stroke occurs, ATP binds to detach, ATP hydrolysis re-cocks head.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Begin with calcium rising in the muscle cytosol. **Ca²⁺ binds troponin**, shifting tropomyosin and making actin sites accessible. An energized myosin head carrying ADP and inorganic phosphate can then interact with actin. Release of phosphate is associated with the force-generating transition, in which the head changes conformation and pulls relative to the thin filament. ADP is subsequently released.

A new ATP molecule binds to myosin and causes **detachment from actin**. Hydrolysis of that ATP then re-cocks the head into an energized state. If calcium remains elevated and an actin site is available, the head can attach again and repeat the cycle. Many heads cycle asynchronously, producing sustained force at the filament level.

Calcium controls access to actin through the regulatory proteins; ATP supports myosin cycling and is specifically necessary for detachment. ATP is also used by SERCA to remove calcium during relaxation, but that is a separate use from the cross-bridge cycle itself.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 36 — E-C coupling {#w06-sr08}

Trace excitation–contraction coupling from a skeletal muscle AP to Ca²⁺ release and contraction.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
AP down T-tubules → voltage sensor activation → RyR opening → SR Ca²⁺ release → Ca²⁺–troponin binding → tropomyosin movement → cross-bridge cycling.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Excitation–contraction coupling connects an action potential in the muscle membrane with activation of the contractile proteins. The muscle action potential spreads along the sarcolemma and enters **T-tubules**, carrying the voltage change deep into the fiber. At triads, voltage sensors in the T-tubule membrane lie next to calcium-release channels in the SR.

Depolarization changes the conformation of the dihydropyridine receptor, the skeletal-muscle voltage sensor. Its mechanical coupling to the ryanodine receptor opens the SR release pathway. Stored calcium enters the cytosol and binds troponin, causing tropomyosin to move so that myosin can bind actin. Cross-bridge cycling then generates force, provided ATP is available.

The skeletal mechanism should be distinguished from cardiac calcium-induced calcium release. In skeletal muscle, the immediate coupling does not depend on extracellular calcium first entering through the L-type channel to trigger SR release.

The action potential does not pull the filaments directly. When excitation ceases, release declines and SERCA lowers cytosolic calcium, reversing the regulatory activation and allowing relaxation.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 37 — Relaxation {#w06-sr09}

Explain skeletal muscle relaxation after motor-neuron firing stops.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
ACh is removed, no new muscle APs occur, SERCA returns Ca²⁺ to SR, Ca²⁺ leaves troponin, tropomyosin blocks actin, cycling stops.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
When motor-neuron firing stops, new action potentials no longer arrive to trigger ACh release. Acetylcholinesterase removes ACh from the synaptic cleft, the end-plate depolarization subsides, and no further muscle action potentials are initiated under normal conditions. Without continuing excitation, SR calcium-release channels no longer sustain the activation signal.

Calcium already present in the cytosol must still be removed. **SERCA uses ATP to pump Ca²⁺ back into the SR**, lowering free cytosolic calcium. Calcium then dissociates from troponin, and the troponin–tropomyosin complex returns toward the state that restricts myosin binding to actin.

As existing cross-bridges detach through ATP binding and fewer new force-generating attachments form, active tension declines. Elastic structures and external loads help determine how the muscle's length changes as it relaxes.

Relaxation requires energy for calcium pumping and cross-bridge detachment; it is not a state achieved just by withdrawing ATP from the cell.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 38 — Force {#w06-sr10}

Explain temporal summation, tetanus, motor-unit recruitment, and the size principle.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Summation adds twitches before full relaxation; high frequency can tetanize; recruitment adds motor units; small units are generally recruited first.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
There are two different ways to increase whole-muscle force: change the activity of fibers already contracting, or add more fibers to the contraction. **Temporal summation** uses the first strategy. A new action potential arrives before the mechanical response to the previous one has fully ended, producing additional calcium release and greater force while some activation persists.

As stimulation frequency rises, less relaxation occurs between responses. The force may show oscillations during unfused tetanus and become relatively smooth during fused tetanus. The individual action potentials remain separate; it is the longer-lasting calcium-dependent mechanical response that sums.

**Motor-unit recruitment** uses the second strategy. Activating additional motor neurons brings their associated muscle fibers into the response. According to the size principle, smaller, lower-threshold units are generally recruited first, followed by larger units as drive and force requirements increase.

Neither requires individual muscle action potentials to become larger, and activating every unit simultaneously would eliminate much of the graded control needed for precise movements.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 39 — Length-tension {#w06-sr11}

Explain the skeletal muscle length–tension relationship in terms of filament overlap.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Force is greatest near optimal overlap; too little overlap limits cross-bridges at long lengths; excessive overlap/interference reduces force at very short lengths.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Active muscle tension depends partly on how many myosin heads can form productive cross-bridges with actin at the fiber's initial length. Near an **optimal sarcomere length**, thick and thin filaments overlap in a configuration that permits many effective interactions, so maximal active force is relatively high.

At long lengths, overlap decreases. Even with normal calcium activation and ATP availability, some myosin heads cannot reach actin, reducing the number of productive cross-bridges. With sufficiently little overlap, active force becomes very small. At excessively short lengths, interference among thin filaments and between filaments and the sarcomere boundaries also reduces useful force generation.

This explanation concerns **active tension generated by cross-bridges**. Passive tension from elastic elements, including titin and connective tissue, tends to increase as a muscle is stretched. Total measured tension can therefore include a growing passive component even when active tension is decreasing. A graph must be interpreted according to which of these quantities it shows.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::

### Question 40 — Application {#w06-sr12}

Predict the effect of a toxin that prevents SR Ca²⁺ release but leaves the motor neuron and NMJ intact.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Muscle APs and end-plate potentials can occur, but cytosolic Ca²⁺ fails to rise adequately, so troponin is not activated and force is greatly reduced/absent.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Locate the toxin's action precisely: it prevents **calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum**, while the motor neuron and neuromuscular junction remain intact. An arriving motor-neuron action potential can therefore still trigger presynaptic calcium entry, ACh release, nicotinic-receptor activation, and an end-plate potential. A muscle action potential can also be generated and propagate along the sarcolemma and T-tubules.

The interruption occurs after electrical excitation reaches the release machinery. Without adequate SR calcium release, cytosolic Ca²⁺ does not rise enough to bind and activate troponin normally. Tropomyosin continues to restrict access to actin sites, so cross-bridge recruitment and force are greatly reduced or absent, depending on the extent of the block.

ATP can support cycling only when the contractile proteins are appropriately activated; it cannot substitute for the calcium-sensitive regulatory switch.

Compare it with nicotinic-receptor blockade: that earlier interruption can prevent the muscle action potential itself, whereas the SR-release block allows excitation but disrupts its conversion into force.

**Course sources:** Lectures 15–17; Silverthorn (2019), Chapters 10 and 12.

**Review:** [Week 6 study guide](../study-guides/week06-vision-muscle.qmd).
:::
